title: Is Harvard Better Than Stanford?
summary: Cherie, just graduated from Stanford GSB, and Jean, seven years out of HBS, compare their MBA experiences: favorite founder-focused classes, how much professors invest in students, why HBS was worth it (organic friendships rather than 'networking'), the case method and cold-calling versus GSB's mixed formats, and why an elite MBA acts as an 'unspoken totem' that makes women in male-dominated tech and finance less dismissable.

ideas.idea: The best business school classes are defined by professors who genuinely care about students, not just by content.
ideas.detail: Jean's favorite HBS class was Founder's Dilemmas with Shikhar Ghosh, who built and sold $100M companies yet gave every student a book with a personalized note; the class became a close-knit community she still draws friends from.

ideas.idea: Make the effort to get to know your professors in grad school; given the opportunity they will invest in you, including hosting students for dinners at their homes.
ideas.detail: Jean's one regret from HBS was not knowing more professors, so she told Cherie to prioritize it at GSB; small classes make one-on-one relationships possible, unlike 300-person undergrad lectures.

ideas.idea: Both schools now offer founder-lifecycle courses covering everything from co-founder chemistry to IPO or acquisition decisions.
ideas.detail: Cherie took Formation of New Ventures at GSB with Jim Ellis, Patricia Nakache and Scott Brady; the HBS corollary is Scaling Tech Ventures with Jeff Bussgang, and entrepreneurship curriculum has expanded greatly since Jean graduated.

ideas.idea: HBS was worth it, but not for the expected reasons: the real payoff is a set of organic friendships with ambitious people who naturally peer-mentor each other.
ideas.detail: Jean almost turned HBS down because trusted Silicon Valley mentors said it would waste valuable career time; seven years later most of her closest friends are from HBS and she expects to keep making friends-of-friends through it.

ideas.idea: 'Networking' needs redefining: at business school it is simply friendship with people who share interests and want to help each other succeed.
ideas.detail: The hosts find the word icky (LinkedIn as 'the networking platform', 'networking events') and say career talk comes up naturally because everyone thinks building companies is fun; Thursday-night beer pong league at GSB counts.

ideas.idea: HBS relies entirely on the case method with cold-calling, which makes class preparation far more intense than at GSB where formats range from lectures to relaxed workshops.
ideas.detail: Every HBS class of about 90 students requires reading a mini research paper about a company and being ready to be picked at random to argue, for example, why a CEO chose VC fund A over B; it was obvious and comical when someone had not read the case.

ideas.idea: The case method works because you put yourself in the protagonist's shoes and decide what you would do, accumulating hundreds of snapshots of business decisions.
ideas.detail: After the discussion you learn what the CEO actually did and why, then reflect on why you chose differently and what to apply going forward.

ideas.idea: For a woman in male-dominated tech and finance, an elite MBA is an 'unspoken totem' that nobody in the room can take away and that gets people to take the call.
ideas.detail: Jean quotes her former CMO; people may know nothing else about you, but Harvard or Stanford on the resume adds credibility to everything you say.

ideas.idea: People are often looking for a reason to dismiss a woman in business, and a grad degree makes you less dismissable; it is wrong, but it is the reality.
ideas.detail: Cherie says the stamp adds immediate credibility with people who have never met you, and hopes the dynamic changes.

ideas.idea: Credentials matter more if you were not 'born on third base'; elite alumni networks and even a .edu email open doors for people without inherited access.
ideas.detail: Analogy from one of Cherie's professors; the hosts joke about getting a PhD just to keep the .edu address.
